Now, I have a question for you. You’ve written two books analyzing and thinking about conservatives: The Reactionary Mind and The Enigma of Clarence Thomas. People have asked me what it feels like to “spend time” with people like Laxman whose behaviors or opinions one abhors. What is it like for you as a writer and theorist?

Robin: Until recently it wasn’t a problem. I enjoyed living with, being with, studying people who initially seemed distant and strange, even abhorrent. They felt like people who had to be figured out. Everybody has a story, which can turn into a shtick. The trick is to get inside it. And it felt like a challenge to translate what I’d found back to people who are not on the right. As with all travel writing, I had to bring these “foreign” elements back home.

But something has changed for me since the rise of Trump. I find it almost impossible to understand the anti-immigrant and xenophobic elements of the right. I don’t have an ounce of nationalism or patriotism, but the one element of American history that stirs me emotionally—the one thing that I think the United States, for all its faults, once got right—is immigration. Seeing how immigrants are always reinventing and retelling the American story, making it more alive and more present, I genuinely don’t understand how can people be against that.

A bigger challenge for me is that the right today is mostly derivative and unimaginative. When I read the right, I don’t see or hear much, at the deepest levels, that I haven’t seen or heard before. And I see a lot of scholars and journalists with a bottomless appetite for that derivativeness, and I can’t work myself up to the enthusiasms of their reading. Part of what I was drawn to in your novel is that even if the political landscape is familiar, the psychic landscape is not. It’s filled with new minds and surprises, and things blowing up in unexpected ways.

Mahajan: I wonder, though, when I hear you talk about a block, whether the xenophobic right is a subject you will end up writing about precisely because you find it hard to comprehend.

Robin: That may be a bridge too far for me.

Mahajan: What was the entry point for you into the mind of Clarence Thomas in The Enigma of Clarence Thomas?

Robin: Thomas has a story that’s rooted in the experience of the Ivy League, which is a story of humiliation and of resentment that’s familiar to me, even though he tells it through the paradigm of race and thinks that’s the only paradigm in which it can be understood. When people on the left, particularly white people, “otherize” Thomas by saying,“His whole politics of resentment is just about being snubbed at Yale,” I think, “Can’t you identify with that at all?” On the other hand, Thomas is this total narcissist who really does seem to think humiliation never happened to anyone but him.

Mahajan: In writing about figures like Thomas or Laxman, there is an automatic tension that comes into play because they have already been identified as “bad” by those most likely to read your work. Do you think that generates a frisson?

Robin: Yes, but maybe not in the way you’re getting at. There are moments in the writing where I’m inhabiting the mind of, let’s say, Thomas, and reconstructing his arguments, and I suddenly feel lift-off from the immediate evidence that’s in front of me. It feels like flying. I don’t think it’s a moral frisson, an excitement that I’m with the bad boy or something like that. It’s more like: This is somebody who is illegible to many people, and I’m rendering that person intelligible but without that simple script. To me that feels like writing.

Based on the way you deal with Laxman, I think we both know that monsters aren’t interesting if you render them as monsters.

Mahajan: I want to come back to what you said about travel. For example, I’ve noticed that, in my fiction writing, I’m not interested directly in the facts of my own life. Instead, I’m drawn to certain subjects or images in an inexplicable way. Writing about individuals with different ideologies is a version of that. I wonder if you feel less excited writing about people who are in the same ideological realm as you are because you already agree with and understand them.

Robin: Definitely. I feel that most when I’m teaching. My teaching is best when I’m dealing with writers who are not like me. The ones who are like me, I have a hard time making them interesting and worth reading. And I think that’s partly why, for many years, I stayed away from writing about the left. It’s not that I don’t think about myself and the ideas I share with the left. It’s that whenever I try to render them on the page, they feel inert.

Mahajan: Now I want to pose a moral question. Obviously, what one doesn’t want to do, as a writer, is revel in the evil or badness of a character or the worst instincts of the right. This is a point Coetzee makes in “The Problem of Evil” in Elizabeth Costello. As a novelist, my own strategy has been to inhabit my “bad” characters very physically and to let their objectionable behaviors emerge sideways, through their actions. A character’s racism, for example, wouldn’t be the center of the frame, because making it central is what the person who is viewing them as a racist is doing. But when you say that you want to “see the world through [Thomas’s] eyes,” how do you avoid the problem of, say, overly sympathizing with his views?

Robin: As you were talking, I thought of Hannah Arendt, in her portrait of Eichmann. This is exactly what she does and always gets attacked for. She writes, for example, about how, at the end of the war, when all the Nazis are trying to figure out what’s going to happen to them, Eichmann’s obsessed about whether Kaltenbrunner, who’s his senior, is going to invite him to lunch. Yet he has no memory of all these details of a transport in which tens of thousands of people were killed. People thought that Arendt was trying to diminish Eichmann’s evil, but I think she was trying to do what you’re describing: to find a way into the being of somebody who could perpetrate such crimes.

With Thomas, it wasn’t so hard, because he does it for you. In his memoir, he begins with the food that he ate in Pinpoint, this particular kind of crab and different kinds of seafood. He tells you the music he was listening to at critical moments in his life, what he was wearing. From those details and others, you begin to get a picture of someone who is definitively placed somewhere in time, who has specific tastes and preferences, distinctive dispositions, in the way all people do, that don’t tell you about his politics but do give you a feeling for him as a person. From there you start thinking about how such a person, in this case, Thomas, moves through the world as a Black man, yet says and does things that make life terrible for Black people.

Going back to Elizabeth Costello, I want to emphasize what you said, about not reveling in the evil. This is a huge problem. It’s not just an aesthetic problem; it’s a political problem. It’s one of the things that I’ve always hated about left-wing writing about the right, which is that it seems to revel in the right’s evil. But it’s a bigger challenge now. We have this cesspool in the White House, and I see the way people on the left love to talk about it. Every horrible detail. It’s a dead end—it’s like enjoying a horror movie; it’s not really thinking about what’s going on there. The alternative isn’t letting it go, maintaining silence about it, but taking those details as signs of something other than movie-level monstrosity, using them as a beginning for understanding something we didn’t understand before.

Mahajan: What are the other common mistakes that novelists and theorists make when writing about reactionaries?

Robin: There are two, and both speak to how well you write about the right. Judith Shklar, the political theorist at Harvard, wrote a book called Ordinary Vices. Her second chapter is about hypocrisy and why we hate it. But she takes great pains to remind us that hypocrisy is not the worst vice. I never appreciated her point until recently, but it’s useful advice for thinking about the right. The right’s hypocrisy often gives the left orgasms. The left always needs to relearn the lessons of Hegel and Marx—beneath any surface contradiction, there’s a complex and elusive unity. It’s our job to find it, not to dwell on the contradiction or hypocrisy, because dwelling on it keeps the unity in obscurity.

The other mistake involves how we deal with sex and shame. There’s an easy story to tell about the right’s sexual morality, which is that it derives from repressed “deviance,” that is from repressing desires that the right deems deviant yet members of the right still feel, only more so. It’s a convenient script that tells you little. Most people, across the spectrum, have all kinds of shame associated with sex. It’s part of what sex is, it’s part of what often creates desire. One of the virtues of your novel is how intelligently it deals with the subjects of sex and shame.

Mahajan: For me, my novels don’t work till I have the characters’ sexual drives figured out. I experienced this with my characters in The Association of Small Bombs as well. At the time, the larger discourse around Islamic fundamentalism was so puerile that it made my task easier in some ways. The idea that fundamentalists were committing terrorist attacks because they didn’t have sex! It’s shocking that this was a mainstream view.

But that brings me to the next question, which was the one about novels. You’ve written, “Politicians and parties talk of constitution and amendment, natural rights and inherited privileges. But the real subject of their deliberations is the private life of power…. It is also why it has so often fallen to our novelists to explain to us our politics.” Were there specific novelists you were thinking about or reading for The Reactionary Mind and The Enigma of Clarence Thomas?

Robin: There are some classics that inspired The Reactionary Mind, one of which is The Leopard. But the truth is: there aren’t a lot of great novels on the chaos of reactionary thought, and I think the reason can be found in our society’s vision of politics.

In Britain, Macaulay famously writes, “Government exists for the purpose of keeping the peace.” Compare that to Hegel, in Germany, who writes that “all the worth which a human being possesses, all spiritual reality, he possesses only through the state.” For a lot of Anglo-American political writers, government and politics are limited in scope, an instrument for keeping the peace. I think this is why we’ve had a tough time, particularly in the US, with political novels, whether of the radical or reactionary variety. I don’t think it’s an accident that the greatest political novels in the US are by Black authors, like Morrison and Ellison, for whom politics is closer to what it was for Hegel, that is, for whom it’s clear that politics weighs upon all of our inner lives, our entire spiritual reality.

I wonder how this maps out for you in India. My sense from your novel is that weaving politics into the personal is not nearly as difficult there as it is here. Is that true?

Mahajan: Yes, but that’s because of an inversion of that Macaulay quote about government existing solely to keep the peace. When a government fails at basic tasks, it is suddenly everywhere in the lives of its citizens. To paraphrase Hegel, one’s spirituality is forcibly squeezed through the toothpaste tube of the state. And the history of government in India has been one of massive failures—corruption, infrastructural collapses, bureaucratic delays—which press down on the daily lives of individuals even in the middle and upper classes. Indians are more political because they have no choice but to be political.

Then there’s history. Most people in India are only two or three generations removed from the upheavals of India’s independence and partition. As a Punjabi from Delhi, for example, I can still connect certain social attitudes toward women or Muslims to the violence of partition. American literature would feel quite different if the War of Independence was just in the rearview mirror.

A more cynical part of me worries that the Indian political novel has hardened into a genre—here’s a person, here’s a riot, here’s a sprinkling of postcolonial history. But a genre that attempts to capture the nexus of the personal and the political is preferable, in my mind, to the autobiographical evasions of so much American fiction, which simply replicates the atomization of American life without confronting its causes. Make American writing political again!

entries.title: Boxcar to Nowhere
entries.summary: American lore about hoboes has sugared over the economic and environmental forces that drove people from their homes and onto the rails and roads in the first place, as a new history lays out.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
A hundred years ago, it seemed as if everyone wanted to be a hobo, at least if you were listening to the radio. Carl Sandburg’s 1927 American Songbag featured a whole section of hobo songs presenting the bum as a beau ideal. Children, most of whom would never see the inside of a boxcar, grew up singing “Hallelujah, I’m a Bum!,” recorded first by Harry McClintock in 1928 and repopularized by the New Christy Minstrels in the 1960s. Along with loads of other songs, it celebrated the paradoxical appeal of the rails and the open road: freedom allied with loneliness and destitution. John Lee Hooker’s “Hobo Blues,” Jimmie Rodgers’s “Hobo Bill’s Last Ride,” and Merle Haggard’s cover of Rodgers’s “Hobo’s Meditation” would become landmarks of the genre. The album cover of Haggard’s I’m a Lonesome Fugitive (1967) depicts him climbing aboard a freight car, a look of consummate fulfillment on his face.

Dreams of a tramp utopia, once termed “hobohemia,” produced classics of Americana.1 Recorded in the 1920s by McClintock, the rollicking hobo anthem “Big Rock Candy Mountain” envisions an itinerants’ paradise where cigarette trees bloom and streams of alcohol trickle down the rocks. It has since been recorded or performed by dozens of folk, pop, and country musicians, including Pete Seeger, Burl Ives, Bing Crosby, Tex Ritter, Johnny Cash, Roger Whittaker, the Highwaymen, and the Nashville string band Old Crow Medicine Show. Its sly salute to sin has become a hallmark of this particular form of counterculture: Wallace Stegner named a novel after the song, and it features prominently in the Coen brothers’ satirical adaptation of the Odyssey set in the American South, O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000), itself an homage to an earlier hobo film, Preston Sturges’s 1941 Sullivan’s Travels.

The contradictory nature of the hobo, a character without home or possessions who embodied good-natured liberty and a gap-toothed joie de vivre, gave rise to a persistent sense of envy. As a result, Woody Guthrie’s fictionalized 1943 autobiography, Bound for Glory, exaggerated the extent of his riding the rails, and he would lean heavily on the bindle stiff gospel throughout his life and career, disappearing for weeks at a time after telling his wife he was going out for cigarettes. In one song he claimed, “I ain’t got no home in this world anymore”; in another he described the afterlife of a “Backdoor Bum”; in yet another he denounced “Old Man Trump,” the president’s father and Guthrie’s landlord in Brooklyn, for “racial hate.” His most famous song, “This Land Is Your Land,” remains an impassioned denunciation of private property and a hymn to the “freedom highway,” its pointed lyrics encouraging wanderers to flout the law:

As I went walking I saw a sign there,

And on the sign it said “No Trespassing.”

But on the other side it didn’t say nothing.

That side was made for you and me.

Shortly after arriving in New York City in 1961, Bob Dylan cast himself as Guthrie’s protégé, devouring Bound for Glory “cover to cover like a hurricane” and identifying so strongly with his mentor that he told a public relations flack at Columbia Records, his newly acquired label, that he’d made his way across country to the Big Apple in hobo fashion as if it were a career qualification. His 2004 memoir recalls the exchange:

“How did you get here?” he asked me.

“I rode a freight train.”

“You mean a passenger train?”

“No, a freight train.”

“You mean, like a boxcar?”

“Yeah, like a boxcar. Like a freight train.”

“Okay, a freight train.”

Dylan was a latter-day fabulist in the mold of Mark Twain, calling himself a “migrant worker” and claiming that he’d once worked for a circus. In fact he rode to New York in the backseat of an acquaintance’s ’57 Impala. Yet in his early days his impulse to establish street cred as a tramp was so intense that he told the folk singer Ramblin’ Jack Elliott, who suspected the younger singer of borrowing from Guthrie, that he had “learnt…songs from various hoboes he met on the road.” Elliott drily noted, “I didn’t argue about it.”

These colorful anecdotes, alongside the hobo songs Dylan began writing or performing (“I Am a Lonesome Hobo,” “Only a Hobo,” and “Freight Train Blues”), are reflections of the conflicted national character already present in Walt Whitman’s “Song of the Open Road”—“Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road…the world before me”—and of course “Song of Myself,” our euphoric yawp to individualism, independence, self-reliance, and the worship of oceanic open spaces:

I tramp a perpetual journey (come listen all!)

signs are a rain-proof coat, good shoes, and a staff cut from the woods….

Not I, not any one else can travel that road for you

You must travel it for yourself.

As with the troubadours who followed, the Good Gray Poet hints that the rewards of the road and its journey to self-awareness may come at the cost of poverty and isolation.

Advertisement

High-spirited songs often cast hobo life as upbeat and fancy-free, but literary works on the theme were likely to involve grim accounts of penury and abuse: in Jack London’s 1907 memoir, The Road, a forerunner of Jack Kerouac, he describes getting picked up for vagrancy in Erie County, New York, and subsisting on bread and water while serving on a chain gang. John Steinbeck’s Of Mice and Men (1937) and The Grapes of Wrath (1939) were based in part on a series of articles he wrote in 1936 for The San Francisco News, “The Harvest Gypsies,” about the lives of migrant laborers who followed the harvest during the Great Depression. Capturing the dangers faced by these antiheroes as they dodged railroad police wielding billy clubs or ranch managers with guns, these accounts immersed the reader in the subjective sensory musk of the experience: the smoke of barrel fires, the pungent character of the slang, the desperate sweat of a Yankee Doodle strain of nostalgie de la boue.

What these distinctly American stories do not address, however, are the hard-to-discern economic and environmental forces that drove people from their homes and onto the rails and roads in the first place. Historians have long identified the aftermath of the Civil War as the origin, when homeless or wounded veterans looking for employment formed a “great army of tramps.” Some reach back further, interpreting colonial America as a “surplus” population from the old country, sent to the New World as a “solution to…the homelessness crisis of Tudor and Stuart England.”2

The Dust Bowl and the Great Depression have been seen as a major impetus behind the mass migrations of the 1930s, but less attention has been paid to the depression and the dust bowl of the 1890s and the wave of farm failures they produced, their boom-and-bust years signaling catastrophes to come. For that we have Robert Suits’s The Hobo: A History of America’s First Climate Migrants, a modern reassessment of the long road this country has traveled toward climate disaster and homelessness. In this punctilious work, we learn that hoboes were far from the simple stereotypes of the carefree, careworn, or hapless wanderers of song and story. They were, in fact, some of the hardest-working people out there.

According to Suits, the idea of the hobo (the etymology of the word is uncertain) emerged as soon as there were coal- or steam-powered engines. During boom years, migrant workers provided the muscle to serve the massive industrialized agriculture machine that settlers began busily erecting in the Midwest and the Great Plains as soon as they arrived on the scene. Manual labor was essential in what he calls our “climatically unstable hinterlands,” largely because early forms of mechanization, such as horse- or steam-powered threshing machines, left gaps in the system that could be filled only by human hands.

During good years, it was hoboes who were reaping, binding, winnowing, and threshing the American wheat crop. The low population density of the Dakotas, Kansas, and Oklahoma meant there were not enough farmers or resident laborers living in the Great Plains to perform necessary work. While some estimates put the number of homeless people in the early 1900s at half a million, from 1870 to 1930 there were between 100,000 and 200,000 itinerant workers—and this at a time when “migrant work, homelessness, and radicalism intertwined,” Suits writes. Around 1910, 100,000 were laboring in the intensive wheat-growing areas of Minnesota, the Dakotas, and Kansas while tens of thousands worked as lumbermen in the North Woods of Wisconsin and Minnesota. Thousands more worked in mines in Illinois, in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and throughout the West. There were few in the South, where white supremacy held sway and labor was supplied mainly by sharecroppers. Hoboes were largely men, although 3 percent were women performing domestic labor, cooking and sewing for agricultural crews or in lumber camps. Small numbers of women also worked wheat harvests—a fact that male journalists found surprising.

Hoboes defined themselves as homeless, migratory, and seeking work. “Chasing the harvest,” they called it, looking to distinguish themselves from “tramps” or “bums” who eschewed labor and were perhaps stationary, hunkering down in towns or cities and presumably begging or stealing to get by. Communities and property owners paid little attention to such distinctions, even as employers desperate for migrant labor begged in newspaper advertisements for hands to bring in the crops or work coal seams.

The moment migrant laborers were no longer wanted, communities turned on them. Suits tells the illustrative story of the hoboes’ shifting fates in the Dakotas and the Northern Plains of the 1890s. The first year of the decade was relatively poor for wheat; 1891 was a record harvest. The following year promised to be even better, with grain fattening on reliable rains resulting from atmospheric lows and with little in the way of hail, floods, or damaging winds. In 1892 the bumper crop was so heavy that employers began panicking at the need for hands to haul it in.

Advertisement

Farmers greeted trains that year, offering “harvest hands” more than two dollars per day plus room and board (women were offered only two dollars a week to feed the men), and for the first time the railroads themselves reduced or waived fares on major trunk lines in an attempt to lure “teachers, businessmen, and even circuit court judges”—hoping to abet the transport of lucrative carloads of grain. That year there were barely enough workers to complete the harvest before it spoiled. Farmers and their hobo workforce produced 70 million bushels of wheat, “one for every citizen in the United States.”

The year 1893 was a different story. A drought year, it was a “nightmare,” Suits says, followed by year after year of drought, the worst period until the 1930s. At the same time, the price of wheat fell owing to a global wheat glut and an economic depression. Once-valued itinerant laborers were cast adrift, dismissed as lazy and shiftless and increasingly seen as a threat to towns and families. Where once “harvest hand” was an affectionate term for newborn babies, “tramps” were now denounced as dirty drunks. Newspapers reviled them in moral terms, hinting at fears that tramp life offered, in Suits’s words, “a haven for homosexuality and nonnormative behaviors” that would imperil women and children. The drought alone didn’t cause this violent shift in rhetoric, but the surplus of workers engendered by boom-and-bust eventually incited violence against homeless men. “The increasing suspicion of the harvest hand,” Suits argues, arose from “climatic conditions and the economic and penal systems around them.”

What emerges as a theme in The Hobo is the sheer nastiness of townsfolk, police, railroad bulls, and farmers themselves in dealing with the “tramp problem,” a viciousness baked into small-town attitudes since the Puritans gave shape to our national identity, with its moral superiority and hostility toward outsiders. “Police turfed hoboes from cars, criminals shot and beat them for their earnings, and on top of all that, farmers increasingly saw hoboes as employees and adversaries rather than friendly faces at the dinner table,” Suits writes. Even when they were working, they were suspected of loose morals and alcoholism.

In 1913 an editorial in The Mirror, a newspaper published by Minnesota’s Stillwater State Prison, described harvest hands who expected “a large drink of whiskey every morning,” two lunches carried to the field, and a “quart bottle of beer at dinner.” Not perhaps unreasonable for people doing hard labor in the fields from dawn to dusk—“killing work,” one called it—but the gracious meeting of these needs by a “Bohemian farmer” suggests how different self-righteous American pieties regarding alcohol and abstinence could be from somewhat more relaxed European attitudes. The writer noted that experienced hands returned to the same Bohemian settlement year after year: “The best harvest hands are hoboes, they do the work; but to keep them with you, they have to be treated according to their standard. The hobo’s idea of a good time is to have plenty of things to drink.”

The volatility of responses to harvest workers gave rise to a movement to unionize. In the 1910s Joe Hill, a so-called Wobbly, took up a popular vaudeville song, “Ta-Ra-Ra-Boom-De-Ay,” and recast the lyrics to promote the Industrial Workers of the World, which also adopted “Hallelujah, I’m a Bum!” as its anthem. In Hill’s version a worker drops his pitchfork, accidentally on purpose, into the cogs of the thresher machine, producing an unholy racket and a work shutdown: “Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay!/It made a noise that way.” It was an early version of what we would now call monkeywrenching.

Organizing strikes virtually every year, the IWW managed to raise harvest hand wages to four dollars per day in some parts of the Dakotas by 1917, but its actions became pitched battles between town vigilantes, ad hoc militias, and union organizers. Eventually the gains were threatened by increasing farm mechanization and a federal crackdown during World War I, when threats to the national food supply were characterized as antiwar and union “agitators” were swept up and arrested. Despite their obstreperousness and resistance to organization, hoboes were nonetheless involved in most of the major labor actions of their time. “The heart of our trouble today,” wrote one such radical, “lies in our having allowed private ownership in the big industries of the country.”

For many hoboes, wheat farming occupied summer and fall, lumbering the winter, but felling trees won them no respect either. Robert Frost’s early hobo poem in North of Boston (1914), “The Death of the Hired Man,” adopted the farmers’, not the laborers’, perspective, and his ambiguous response to vagrants is evident in a later work, “Two Tramps in Mud Time”:

Out of the woods two hulking tramps

(From sleeping God knows where last night,

But not long since in the lumber camps).

They thought all chopping was theirs of right.

Men of the woods and lumberjacks,

They judged me by their appropriate tool.

Except as a fellow handled an ax

They had no way of knowing a fool.

Arguably a bit hulking himself, Frost grudgingly acknowledges the tramps’ “need” as a “better right,” but he keeps on chopping, insisting that his purpose, “to unite/My avocation and my vocation,” is higher. The poet known for his dialogues chooses not to give them a voice.

Suits is at his sharpest when writing about the North Woods of Wisconsin, the legendary Big Woods that stretched across thousands of acres of the great Northland. He grew up among the scars concealed by a canopy of second growth,

wounds that have barely begun to heal…. You can see the past…in how nearly every tree is the same size; there were no old oaks or maples on my childhood street. Each of them, without exception, was not yet a century old.

Eloquent on the risks of felling massive trees and skidding logs down frozen rivers, he dissects an economy that relied on “raw” human kinetic energy to convert forests into lumber, with men functioning as metabolic engines, working shirtless in the freezing cold as they burned off enormous meals of five, six, or eight thousand calories a day. “A 1910 estimate of power use in the timber industry,” he says, “combined with what we know about camp food suggests humans probably supplied around a third of the total power,” itself perhaps an underestimate. Not surprisingly, Suits notes, hoboes often compared themselves to “draft animals,” lamenting the “horse work” they were required to perform.

Such labor was rewarded with disgusting living conditions: bunkhouses furnished with dirt floors, no ventilation, and verminous blankets. Men like those in Frost’s poem took to the roads searching for better conditions. P.K. Small, a lumberjack interviewed by a federal investigator, was missing half of his nose and had broken a hand, a leg, and a shoulder in various skidding accidents but said he dreaded the bunkhouses the most. Monotonous meals of salt pork or salt beef were filled out with bread or potatoes; drinking water was unsafe, with men sharing a common cup; typhoid fever, smallpox, and influenza were rampant. Accidents were greeted with shrugs. “A drowning did not even slow up the work,” according to a lumberjack in Wisconsin. “The drive had to go on.” Another man, ill with tuberculosis, said, “I got to keep on going till I drop. Every night I think I’m going to die.” Broken limbs and amputations were not uncommon, but there was no recourse for the maimed: private insurance policies excluded lumbering, along with mining and construction work. Such men generally ended up indigent, living in almshouses or begging for food.

The land was also broken: “The woodland that built most of the cities and towns of the Great Plains, from Chicago to tiny farmsteads in Montana, still has yet to regenerate fully, more than a century later.” Towns in the Northland with economies once dependent on lumber were left to shift to other forms of income or simply disappear.

Hoboes themselves began to vanish. Tractors and increasingly sophisticated forms of automation took their places on farms, and the North Woods were logged out by 1920. Lumberjacks moved on to lay waste to the Pacific Northwest and the pine forests of the South, and there, too, mechanization began replacing human labor. Successive union strikes helped to establish an eight-hour workday in northwestern lumber camps and mills, but by the 1950s the chainsaw took the place of axes and handsaws, and cars made commuting to lumber jobs possible for family men.

By the mid-twentieth century, the Great Plains were growing “wheat sick,” with yields depleted by years of monoculture. To meet the needs of farmers raising fruit in California and the sugar beets that were replacing wheat in the Midwest, families from Mexico were recruited in the border states, with some moving north to handle the beet crop. Asked by Congress why they were relying on immigrant labor, farmers admitted that Americans didn’t want to do manual labor anymore. Immigrants, meanwhile, found conditions as dirty, dangerous, and exploitative as the hoboes had and were likewise subjected to punitive violence, now embedded in the federal response of ICE.

There is no “clean end” to the history of hoboes, Suits says. Migrant manual laborers still fill what he calls “the interstices of the fossil economy,” the places where human hands are indispensable: they labor in slaughterhouses or in construction jobs or as pickers “in the vast warehouses of online retailers.” In fields, they tend and harvest apples, apricots, avocados, blueberries, carrots, cherries, chiles, grapes, lettuce, melons, mushrooms, raspberries, strawberries, and tomatoes. Yet these workers, “now racialized,” who fill grocery shelves are unceasingly devalued, with Republicans calling for “MASS DEPORTATION NOW!” at their national convention in 2024.

The capitalist system that produced and took advantage of hoboes is still visible today in the new hobo camps—tent cities under highway overpasses where the migrant poor, some 40 percent of whom are working (often two or three jobs), find temporary shelter. If today we were to ask, “O brother, where art thou?” the answer would be simple: a car in the Walmart parking lot. Even if you have a full-time job there, at the base pay of fourteen dollars an hour it would be impossible to afford housing or basic needs. Meanwhile, so-called right-to-work laws limiting union membership in twenty-six states have crippled organizations that might once have lobbied for higher pay and better conditions.

Suits acknowledges that the hoboes’ way of life was shaped by agricultural forces that no longer hold sway. But he points out that we nonetheless inherited from a previous century our heartless attitudes toward homeless and migratory workers and the rhetoric we use to revile them. The number of homeless people in the US, more than 745,000 as of 2025, is “roughly equal” to what it was then, even though the overall population has tripled. Yet the contempt for those who perform our killing work remains a testament to the nature of American generosity. There’s no hallelujah about it.

No one, it seems, envies the hobo or the homeless anymore. Dylan, our great troubadour of the open road, continues to lead a wandering life, restlessly touring year after year. He was scheduled to perform in Las Vegas in 2016 when the Nobel Committee announced that he’d won the prize for literature. He said nothing about the honor to his audience that night and did not respond to the committee for weeks. For an encore, though, he sang a Frank Sinatra song, perhaps an homage to his humblest idols:

I’m sentimental, so I walk in the rain

I’ve got some habits even I can’t explain

Could start for the corner, turn up in Spain

But why try to change me now?

entries.title: Let a Hundred Websites Bloom
entries.summary: The Internet and the smartphone have become formidable tools for the Chinese government to maintain tight control over society.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
When I arrived in Shanghai in the early 2000s to begin a half-decade assignment covering China, I often marveled at the distance between the common Western image of the country as a repressive dictatorship and the many spaces for communication that seemed to escape the government’s control. My first inklings of this came in random encounters with Chinese people, in bank lines, on trains, or on the sidelines of public events. They were as curious about the world that had produced me as I was about the world that had produced them. Moreover, many seemed as disinclined to pull punches in expressing criticism of their society as I was of mine.

These early impressions quickly deepened as I began to explore the country’s Internet. Certainly there were clear taboos, beginning with questioning the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party and criticizing the country’s central leadership. Alongside these topics were the forbidden so-called big Ts: Tibet, Taiwan, and Tiananmen. But surprisingly large realms of online speech remained wide open. Without too much effort, one could find public threads about almost anything else. And people used bulletin boards and discussion groups on Chinese Web platforms like Weibo and QQ to report official malfeasance or corruption at the local or regional level.

During my first years in China, much of my time was spent covering localized protests that gathered strength online. Municipal and provincial officials worked tirelessly to suppress the amplification of whistleblowing and dissent, but the surge in accountability activism and citizen journalism that the early Internet brought to the country reduced their efforts to a futile game of whack-a-mole. Often all that Web-based activists needed to do to evade sanction during local crackdowns was to temporarily set themselves up in a nearby province.

A similar laxity existed about online name verification. Back then there were few practical obstacles to using assumed names on the Web. Those who sought an extra layer of personal security while commenting on risky topics conducted their online life from the grimy and smoke-filled confines of the era’s ubiquitous Internet cafés, where they periodically changed their aliases. Others frequently replaced the SIM cards in their phones.

Once in a while, what began as a very local event would suddenly mushroom into a national outcry over some injustice that hinted at the surviving, if atrophied, democratic potential of a population living under a self-proclaimed dictatorship of the proletariat. That was the case in 2003, the year of my arrival in China, when a twenty-seven-year-old migrant laborer, Sun Zhigang, was arrested in Guangzhou for not carrying proper identification papers and then was beaten to death in detention. The case was heavily covered by the seemingly fearless Southern Metropolis Daily, a muckraking newspaper. But news about it soon spread much farther via the Internet and sparked outrage in viral posts and discussion groups. Almost astoundingly in a country known for strict, top-down control, three months after Sun was killed, the central government dismantled the heavy-handed and secretive national custody system used to detain Chinese workers who violated the country’s strict residential permit system.

In March 2000 Bill Clinton had come close to predicting that the advent of the Web would bring about a radical relaxation of top-down political control in China: “Now, there’s no question China has been trying to crack down on the Internet—good luck. That’s sort of like trying to nail jello to the wall.” Although I wasn’t betting against the possibility that censorship would win out in the long run in China, during my early years there one could still imagine that Clinton might have been right. But that is no longer the case.

Since I left the country, the entire landscape of online life and the political space enjoyed by its citizens have shrunk radically. This has happened in part because of the ubiquitous rise of the smartphone, which has proven to be the perfect tool for state surveillance, censorship, and much more strictly enforced conformity. There are many reasons for this, beginning with the fact that China belatedly began enforcing the requirement to show official identification in order to get SIM cards, which made aliases useless and eliminated the protection of anonymity. What is worse, smartphones make it easy for the state to document their owners’ every movement and communication.

Easily as important as these features, though, has been the astonishingly fast and nearly universal adoption of China’s powerful homegrown app, WeChat, which has established itself as a one-stop clearinghouse for almost everything that non-Chinese smartphone users accomplish with a plethora of apps. In China, people not only chat through WeChat, they also use it as a social media platform, rely on it for news and entertainment, and use it to bank, shop, make travel arrangements, conduct their business, and even pay taxes and government fines. WeChat’s astonishing rise took place not long after I left China in 2008, and its hold on the society is so pervasive that for any outsider like me who wishes to stay in touch with friends there or to navigate the country during visits, maintaining an account and mastering its functions are essential.

Advertisement

The other development of enormous consequence for freedom of speech and the degree of openness in China, of course, has been the ascension of the country’s current leader, Xi Jinping. Since he became president in 2013, the ruling Communist Party has placed an emphasis on social control unseen in China at least since Mao Zedong’s heyday. Mao relied on neighborhood committees to surveil behavior down to the street level and often encouraged family members to inform on one another. But Xi enjoys powers of real-time monitoring that Mao could have never dreamed of.

Xi has also doubled or even tripled down on the once-leaky online censorship system known colloquially as the Great Firewall, which not only polices domestic online communications but is also a powerful filter of information from the outside world. I can’t forget my surprise at glimpsing some of the crude inner workings of the early Great Firewall. When I visited a university in Shanghai in 2006, students ushered me into a control room where dozens of campus volunteers were monitoring the online communications of their peers. After my visit, the university’s party secretary told me sheepishly that this wasn’t something the authorities were interested in advertising.

Nowadays, although armies of Web censors are not altogether obsolete, they take a distant backseat to highly sophisticated automated monitoring and surveillance systems, and every Chinese person I’ve ever known is aware of this and assumes its effectiveness, which deters risky speech. As a result, rather than facilitating political change in China, the Internet and the associated world of the mobile phone have become formidable tools the government uses to maintain tight control over the society.

Yi-Ling Liu came of age just as this tide was shifting. After being raised in Hong Kong, then still a wide-open global city where near-Western levels of personal liberties and the rule of law largely prevailed, she went to Beijing in 2010 to work as an intern for a Chinese media company. Learning about the 1989 Tiananmen massacre as a high school student had fed her interest in China’s history, including in recurrent attempts by both ordinary Chinese citizens and political insiders to spark national reform. After graduating from Yale, she writes in The Wall Dancers: Searching for Freedom and Connection on the Chinese Internet,

I returned to Beijing to live and write, because I still wanted to know—not just what could’ve been changed at the square that day but also what could be changed today and who had the power to do the changing.

Liu’s account differs from most recent writing about China by Western journalists in eschewing assessments of the country based on its elite politics or on insights gleaned from interviews with experts. Western journalists have faced sharply restricted access to China under Xi’s rule. In following the history of Internet activism in China, what Liu offers instead is a bottom-up sense of life and the state of personal freedom in the country. Along the way, something striking happens. Rather than confirming the West’s smugness about its individual liberties and democracy compared to China’s, her book slowly builds to the disquieting conclusion that the crushing power of the Internet is steadily making the United States and China more like each other.

The Wall Dancers serves up any number of milestones—like the Sun Zhigang case—that would be familiar to anyone who has followed the country closely since the 2000s. As she recounts, these culminated in what became known as the Weibo Spring, the name given to a period of extraordinary online activism in 2011 that followed the more familiar Arab Spring of protest and reform movements.

Perhaps the biggest catalyst for that year’s breakout activism was a deadly collision in Wenzhou between one of China’s brand-new bullet trains and another train that was stopped on the same track. The impressively rapid introduction this century of high-speed rail service, by now virtually nationwide, has been a major focus of the government’s nationalist propaganda. The crash officially killed forty people and injured nearly two hundred, making it the world’s third-deadliest high-speed rail collision.

The first post about it on Weibo, which went up almost immediately, was a cry for help by a university student who was a passenger. It was immediately reposted by others, as millions of people turned to the social media platform for a more detailed picture of the crash than the government’s sanitized news offered. What ensued was a dramatic, real-time contest between citizens and censors. The next day the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Propaganda Department issued a terse directive to the country’s media: “Do not question. Do not elaborate. Do not associate.”

Advertisement

This meant that only official accounts of the accident would be allowed to circulate. But citizen skepticism had been boosted by official actions that hinted strongly at a cover-up. These included the prompt burial of the wreckage near the crash site and the failure to publish a list of the victims. The online outcry that followed was so intense that China’s then premier, Wen Jiabao, felt obliged to visit the site and promise a full investigation. “If corruption was found behind this, we must handle it according to law, and we will not be lenient,” he said. Later the railway minister at the time was tried and sentenced to life imprisonment for bribery.

The central government’s inability to suppress citizen grievances that forced an official as high-ranking as Wen to promise justice gave the Wenzhou train crash the feeling of a watershed. For the first time in China, it was becoming possible, it seemed, for citizens to use the Internet to hold their remote and controlling government to account. What the accident seems to have accomplished instead was to make the state even more determined that it would never again be so vulnerable to waves of public outcry spreading online.

Liu’s book distinguishes itself by going far beyond well-known events like this, with rich, extended profiles of individuals who had begun using the Internet to try to build new lives for themselves or to change China during the era when the Internet still seemed to offer the possibility of a freer future. For example, in the late 1990s Ma Baoli, a gay junior policeman in the provincial town of Qinhuangdao, began spending his free time at a new Internet café that had opened near his police station. There he began a process of self-discovery and growing awareness of the existence of large numbers of gay men who, like him, lived in the shadows. He joined online forums like Chinese Men’s and Boy’s Paradise, read online gay fiction, and watched “every gay film he could get his hands on, sobbing over his takeout noodles.”

Using a pseudonym, Ma created a website for gay men, Light Blue Memories. After he primed it with his own stories about unrequited love and loneliness and with melancholy reflections about fleeting youth, it took off. In its early years, Ma was obliged to sustain a guerrilla-style backup operation that could relocate his servers from one municipality to another each time authorities tried to close the website on the grounds of indecency.

As it exploded in popularity, Ma rented space in Beijing, a four-hour train ride from his hometown, and commuted back and forth as he managed his dual identities: police officer and host of a social platform for gay people. In March 2012, though, he made the fateful decision to be featured in a documentary about his website, which prompted a huge and unexpected response. The film was covered positively on the home page of Sohu, one of the country’s biggest news portals. It also prompted an angry summons from his boss, who called Ma’s site humiliating for the police.

Ma resigned from the department the next day and, far from being discouraged, created a dating app for gay men, which he named Blued. It soon rocketed to number nine in downloads from China’s Apple app store. In November 2012 China’s minister of health invited Ma to participate in that year’s World AIDS Day conference in Beijing. There, to his surprise, he found himself face-to-face with Premier Li Keqiang and introduced himself, saying, “Greetings, Premier. I run a gay website.” In a scene that played that night on national television, Li shook his hand without missing a beat and said, “Thank you for your hard work, comrade.”

The story of another of Liu’s characters, Lü Pin, follows a somewhat similar arc. After acquiring a graduate degree in Chinese literature in 1994, she took a job at a stodgy state-run newspaper, China Women’s News. Although she had had little prior interest in women’s issues, Lü underwent a steady awakening and soon found herself chafing at the limits she faced in writing about gender inequality for a quasi-official publication. With her sharpness and drive, she nonetheless rose steadily up the paper’s hierarchy and found herself one step away from the deputy editor’s job at age thirty.

In a decision that shocked friends and colleagues, Lü resigned rather than pursue the promotion. To enter senior management, she would have had to join the Chinese Communist Party, and as someone who identified as part of the “1989 generation”—people who came of age around the time of the Tiananmen demonstrations—this was something she couldn’t do unless the party properly faced up to the history of the massacre there.

Lü then took a job in local government in Gansu, a relatively poor province, where she began writing freelance stories about the condition of women in China. Her goal all along was to reach a general audience, not just specialists and intellectuals, but these stories had a sparse readership. Another national public scandal, however, eventually provided Lü the opportunity to reach many more people.

In May 2009 Deng Yujiao, a twenty-one-year-old waitress in a karaoke club in Hubei province, was cornered in the club’s restroom by two local officials who demanded “special services” from her, meaning sex. When she refused, one of them smacked her in the face with a wad of banknotes, shouting, “Don’t you want money? Would you believe if I am going to beat you to death with money today?” Deng stabbed him in the neck with a fruit knife and called the police as he bled out.

Liu is almost certainly correct when she writes that in the pre-Internet era, this incident would have gotten little attention and Deng would have been convicted of homicide, especially since the victim was an official. Instead it went viral, with citizens expressing outrage over a range of issues, from the hints of official corruption in the wad of cash, to the male presumption of a right to sex, to the imagined impunity of the assailants. Amid a gale of public outcry, the charges were dropped.

That September, fired up by these events, Lü founded Women’s Voices, a digital magazine dedicated to women’s rights. At a reader’s suggestion, she soon changed the name to Feminist Voices. Lü wrote prolifically, her publication quickly gained traction with readers, and it helped spawn a loose but energized movement with headquarters in a two-bedroom apartment in Beijing that she called the One Yuan Commune. Every summer it hosted open courses on feminism to highly receptive attendees. “Our society does not allow for alternative views—be it about gender, sexuality, or politics—and those with different views find themselves isolated, rejected by the mainstream, with nowhere to go,” Lü later wrote.

With wind in its sails, the women’s movement that Lü helped create became bolder. It staged acts of guerrilla theater, such as a Valentine’s Day demonstration by three young women in Qianmen, one of Beijing’s busiest commercial districts. They dressed in cheap wedding gowns for the occasion, smeared their bodices with lipstick to resemble blood, and brushed their faces with eyeshadow to mimic bruising. “Yes to love, no to violence,” they chanted as they marched, in denunciation of domestic violence.

Liu tells the stories of Lü and Ma as a study in diverging approaches to how citizens inclined toward activism can relate to the state: the one accommodating and the other militant. But neither, any more than the Wenzhou crash, was a true harbinger of reform and opening in China.

Starting from his successful gay dating site, Ma Baoli built a queer entertainment empire that produced television shows and partnered with queer NGOs. But these early successes were deceptive, and Ma’s company eventually provoked a strong backlash from the state. After it produced a Web series about love between two high school boys called Addicted in 2016, China’s media regulators announced a ban on all portrayals of what it called “abnormal sexual relations,” including same-sex relations. Since then Ma has meekly complied, surviving, as Liu writes, by “always staying in the government’s good graces.”

Lü’s dark reckoning came even sooner. In March 2015, while she was visiting New York to attend the United Nations Commission on the Status of Women conference, Chinese police mounted a multicity roundup of five of the core members of her movement. Lü sent hundreds of emails to raise an international protest, and Hillary Clinton and Samatha Power were among those who condemned the arrests. The five were released after thirty-seven days in detention, but Feminist Voices was shut down and Lü was effectively forced into exile. The state, in the end, found ways to foreclose both of their efforts to loosen state control on gender and social mores in China from the bottom up.

During the Xi years another era has closed in China: from roughly 2007 until 2019 the appetite of young Chinese for study overseas, and particularly in the United States, seemed insatiable. In that peak final year, 372,000 Chinese were pursuing degrees in American colleges and universities. The outbreak of Covid-19 reduced this number by about 50,000, but since the end of the pandemic it has continued to drop, reaching 266,000 last year.

Jimmy Carter had made human rights a centerpiece of his foreign policy, including the right of citizens of Communist countries to emigrate. When the issue of emigration arose during Deng Xiaoping’s 1979 White House visit, Deng turned the argument on its head. “Would you like to import ten million Chinese?” he asked. “There is no question like that for China.” In fact, for many years afterward, if never remotely on this scale, China sent large numbers of students abroad, basing its hopes of catching up economically with the West on the education and training of rising numbers of its best students in American schools.

China’s modern economic takeoff, which began under Deng, has far outstripped almost all early expectations, including his. But it was long shadowed by often-stated doubts. Western politicians, pundits, and even economists said that a strategy of absorbing knowledge from overseas might enable China to catch up, but they questioned whether the country could ever become a leader in innovation and intellectual output, especially as long as it had a closed political system.

China’s economy has slowed in recent years, but its innovation across a number of domains, from electric vehicles and batteries to industrial robots, artificial intelligence, and space exploration, has finally quieted skeptics. Nowadays the Chinese government no longer encourages its students to study overseas, a reflection of another enormous achievement: the rapid rise of its own universities as worthy rivals of the best the West has to offer. The decline in the numbers of Chinese studying abroad has been further accelerated by increasingly restrictive immigration policies in the United States under Donald Trump.

In The Highest Exam: How the Gaokao Shapes China, Ruixue Jia and Hongbin Li argue that one of the most important factors in China’s resurgence through education has ironically been the modern implementation of the gaokao, its little-known and widely misunderstood ancient scholarly examination system. The gaokao is a grueling standardized test administered nationally to roughly 13 million students over two or four days each summer. Its core subjects are Chinese language and literature, mathematics, and a foreign language, which usually means English. Students also choose between electives of science or the humanities.

Whereas Liu points to how the Internet, which seemed to promise greater freedom for China, has instead become an apparatus of efficient state surveillance and control, Jia and Li show how an exam system with roots that go back to the Sui dynasty roughly 1,400 years ago and that has often been derided for promoting rote learning now works to motivate academic achievement and channel intellectual talent with surprising efficiency. Their book goes on to argue that the gaokao is instrumental in sustaining positive attitudes toward education in China and in at least tempering social and economic inequality.

The Highest Exam compiles a detailed and often dry account of the history and inner workings of what amounts to China’s national college entrance exam, which also serves as the foundation for a more personal discussion of the authors’ backgrounds. Both now teach at elite American universities. Li grew up in Jilin province and scored well on the gaokao in 1989, putting him on a path to eventually becoming codirector of the Center on China’s Economy and Institutions at Stanford.

Jia’s story is more revealing. She was the unwanted daughter of a mother who put her up for adoption, and she had the good fortune to be raised by a middle school teacher in Shandong province. Her rural elementary school had only three teachers, who kept an irregular schedule because they were also working farmers. Despite this, Jia became an avid reader and developed a precocious understanding that newly mastered Chinese characters were worth their proverbial weight in gold. Her father put it to her, “What would you like your future to look like? Would you like to attend vocational school? High school? The choice is yours.”

What the questions reveal is not only the weight that educational and vocational tracking still has in China but also the extent to which test taking determines individual outcomes. Prompted by her father’s question, Jia began to compile an outstanding exam record and eventually got the fourth-highest score in her high school on the gaokao. This in turn enabled her to attend a well-regarded college in Beijing.

For Jia and Li, the gaokao and the tests that lead up to it are far more than their rough American school test equivalents, like the SAT. They form the background of an all-pervading national culture of performance metrics that give life in China something of the quality of a vast and never-ending meritocratic tournament:

The lowest-level employees in the warehouses of a Chinese grocery store chain, who likely never finished high school, have their packing efficiency ranked and displayed on TV screens. At a major Chinese tech firm, when asked whether the employees were ranked against one another, the manager responded with some puzzlement: “Of course.”

In the United States, where there is a deep but folkloric belief in laissez-faire and what people imagine to be equal opportunity, many would doubtlessly bridle at this sort of thing. Jia and Li stop short of proposing any universal applicability of China’s approach to organizing opportunity, or even its outright superiority. But they are not shy about asserting what they see as its merits.

One, they argue, is that the gaokao and other exams allow China to place a premium on the so-called STEM fields—science, technology, engineering, and mathematics—that have been so crucial to the country’s economic advancement in the post-Mao era. Partly because of this, they argue, the return on investment through education has been very high, albeit hard to measure with exactitude. It is also not without costs: “China’s Einsteins may not even test into elite colleges, in part because they may not score well in the non-STEM fields. After all, the gaokao is a composite score.”

They also see competitive test-taking as a partial brake on the further increase of inequality in China, which is already very high. It is all but impossible to attend one of the top universities—Tsinghua, Peking, or Fudan—without previously attending a top high school. But access to both is determined by test scores, not nepotism. Jia and Li posit this as a meaningful advantage over American university admission patterns:

In China, children from the richest 20 percent of families—in other words, the upper class—are 2.3 times more likely to go to an elite college than those from the poorest 20 percent of families—the lower class. Meanwhile in the United States, students from wealthy families are fully eleven times more likely to attend elite institutions than those from poor families.

The system they describe, despite its brutal methods, produces something that much American education does not: genuine mathematical and logical grounding at an early age. What it sacrifices, Jia and Li concede, are the critical thinking skills that American college students cultivate more effectively, along with “social skills that are extremely valuable and likely to become even more so as many tasks become automated.” America’s education system also offers greater opportunity to a broader cross-section of the society, and it is more forgiving of those who don’t begin establishing a record of academic achievement early in life.

These two books introduce useful cautions against easy thinking about China, where cultural and historical inertia run deep in both politics and education. Technologies like the Internet, which the West has long associated with freer expression, have become means of ever-greater state social guidance and control. On the other hand, even with its rigidities, a system of educational benchmarking with roots in antiquity has thus far been made to serve economic advancement rather handily. What no one can know is how long either of these will have such effects.
